title: How To Avoid Arguing With Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin uses a scripted classroom example—a student protesting a consequence for pushing a classmate—to show how easily teachers get pulled into arguments once they respond to a student's objection. He identifies the real mistake as waiting for a reaction after delivering a consequence, which trains students to expect and produce a response every time. His fix is to deliver the consequence, pause briefly for the student to face you, state it calmly and matter-of-factly, and immediately return to what you were doing without further exchange. He notes this approach must be explicitly taught and modeled early in the year so students internalize it, and offers a fallback for the rare student who follows and argues anyway: repeat the statement once, then let them cool off before a stronger consequence. The article closes by reframing arguing as a behavior the teacher's own habits often invite, rather than something students simply do unprompted.
points: The core mistake that invites arguing is waiting for a student's reaction after delivering a consequence.
The fix: deliver the consequence calmly and factually, then immediately return to what you were doing without further exchange.
This no-argument delivery style must be explicitly taught and modeled early in the school year to become the norm.
For the rare student who follows and argues anyway, repeat the consequence once, then let them cool off before escalating.
Arguing is frequently a byproduct of the teacher's own delivery habits, not simply unprompted student defiance.
quotes: As soon as you answer back, as soon as you respond and try to justify the consequence, you’re in a full-fledged argument.
You see, the mistake the teacher in the above scenario made was waiting for a response. Many, if not most, teachers do this.
But what this does is invite students to do just that. Before you know it, every time you give a consequence, there is an argument.
Calmly, almost robotically, deliver your consequence and then immediately turn back to what you were doing before .

It’s important to note that how you give a consequence must be thoroughly taught and modeled as part of the series of classroom management-related lessons you’ll teach during the first few weeks of each school year.
In most cases arguing is brought on by the teacher, not the student.
